procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated the 26th September, 1976 of the Gauhati High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 18 of 1975.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Sessions Judge convicted the accused under s. 302 IPC and sentenced him to life imprisonment. On appeal, the High Court set aside the order of conviction and acquitted the respondent of the charge.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The State of Assam filed an appeal by special leave against the judgment of the Gauhati High Court.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in setting aside the conviction of the respondent under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and acquitting him of the charge.

facts: The Sessions Judge initially convicted the respondent for murder under Section 302 IPC, relying on the evidence of the deceased's 7-year-old son and dying declarations made by the deceased.
On appeal, the High Court set aside this conviction and acquitted the respondent, finding it unsafe to rely on the dying declarations and the testimony of the child witness.
The State of Assam then appealed the High Court's acquittal to the Supreme Court.
law: The respondent's counsel argued, citing the precedent in 'Madhoprasad v. The State of Madhya Pradesh', that a conviction cannot be based solely on a dying declaration without corroboration.
application: The Supreme Court considered the High Court's reasoning for acquitting the respondent, which was based on the unreliability of the evidence presented (the child's statement and the dying declarations).
The Court also took into account the legal principle regarding the cautious use of uncorroborated dying declarations, as established in the 'Madhoprasad' case.
Although the full reasoning is not detailed in the provided text, the Court's final decision indicates that it agreed with the High Court's assessment of the evidence.
The Supreme Court concluded that the State's appeal against the acquittal was without merit.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court dismissed the State's appeal and upheld the High Court's decision to acquit the respondent. By finding that the appeal must fail, the Supreme Court effectively concluded that the High Court was justified in setting aside the conviction.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in setting aside the conviction of the respondent under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and acquitting him of the charge.
appellant_arguments: A conviction can be based solely on a dying declaration, even if there is no other corroborating evidence on record.
respondent_arguments: The evidence was too meagre and unreliable to sustain the conviction.
The evidence of the child witness was unreliable as he was vacillating, had been tutored, and was not a free agent.
The dying declarations were not safe to rely upon for a conviction.

cases.case_name: Madhoprasad v. The State of Madhya Pradesh
cases.principle: Cited regarding the principle that a dying declaration alone without corroboration cannot be the basis for a conviction, though the Court noted some observations in it were in the nature of obiter dicta.

cases.case_name: Maniappan v. The Statt of Madras
cases.principle: Cited to support the well-settled law that a conviction can be based on a dying declaration.
Cited to support the well-settled law that a conviction can be based on a dying declaration.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Even in the absence of other corroborating evidence, there can be a conviction on the basis of a dying declaration, provided that the Court is satisfied about the truthfulness of the dying declaration and that it is not vitiated in any other manner.
obiter: There is no absolute rule of law, or even a rule of prudence which has ripened into a rule of law, that a dying declaration unless corroborated by other independent evidence, is not fit to be acted upon, and made the basis of a conviction.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The cumulative effect of all the circumstances which weighed with the High Court is that they cast doubt about the truthfulness of the dying declaration. It is not outside the realm of probability that her statement may have been inspired by her uncle and, therefore, it will not be safe to base the conviction of respondent on such a dying declaration.
legal_tests_applied: There can be a conviction on the basis of dying declaration even in the absence of other corroborating evidence but before doing so, the Court has to be satisfied about the truthfulness of the dying declaration.
why_appellant_lost: While the court agreed with the appellant's legal proposition that a conviction can be based on a dying declaration alone, it found that the specific declaration in this case was not sufficiently truthful or reliable to sustain a conviction.
The court found it would not be safe to base the conviction on the dying declaration because the cumulative effect of the circumstances cast doubt on its truthfulness.
why_respondent_won: The court agreed with the High Court that the dying declaration was not safe to rely upon for a conviction.
The cumulative effect of the circumstances cast doubt on the truthfulness of the dying declaration.
The court found it was probable that the deceased's statement may have been inspired by her uncle.
policy_considerations: It is not safe to base a conviction on a dying declaration if its truthfulness is in doubt, particularly when there is a probability of outside influence on the declarant.
